nameStory: The 'cruet' in Cruet Collar-moss refers to the distinctive bottle-shaped spore capsule that sits atop the moss like a tiny glass cruet from a fancy dining set. The 'collar' describes the flared rim at the base of this capsule, which looks remarkably like the decorative collar on an old-fashioned oil or vinegar bottle.
description: Cruet Collar-moss is a small, specialized moss that forms loose patches or scattered individual plants rather than dense mats. The entire plant is typically only about half an inch tall, with the most striking feature being its unique spore capsule that looks like a miniature bottle or flask. This moss is extremely rare in New England, belonging to the unusual dung moss family that has adapted to grow on animal droppings and decaying organic matter.

idTips.label: Sporophytes
idTips.description: The bottle-shaped spore capsule is unmistakable - swollen at the base with a distinct collar or rim, then narrowing to a neck before the cap. When fresh, it has a glossy, almost ceramic-like appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms small, scattered cushions or individual plants rather than continuous mats. Each plant stands alone like a tiny green bottle brush, rarely more than half an inch tall.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, narrow leaves that feel somewhat stiff when dry but become soft and slightly curved when moist. They're arranged spirally around the stem and have a fresh, earthy smell when crushed.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Always found growing on or very near animal dung, decaying organic matter, or nutrient-rich soil. The substrate often has a distinctive musty, barnyard-like odor.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright to yellowish-green when moist, becoming duller olive-green when dry. The spore capsule ranges from pale green to amber-brown as it matures.

habitat: This extremely rare moss is found in nutrient-rich locations, typically growing directly on herbivore dung or heavily fertilized soil in pastures, barn areas, or places where large animals congregate. In New England, look for it in old farmyards, near livestock areas, or on hiking trails where horses or cattle pass regularly. It prefers partial shade and consistently moist conditions.

seasonality.spring: Young sporophytes begin developing, appearing as tiny green swellings. Plants become more vibrant green as moisture increases and growth resumes after winter dormancy.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for mature sporophytes with fully developed bottle-shaped capsules. This is the best time for identification when the distinctive cruet shape is most prominent and visible.
seasonality.fall: Sporophytes may persist but begin to darken and deteriorate. Plants remain green but growth slows as temperatures drop and daylight decreases.
seasonality.winter: Plants remain present but less conspicuous, often appearing brownish-green. Sporophytes from the previous season may still be visible but are usually weathered and less distinctive.

funFact: Cruet Collar-moss has evolved specifically to launch its spores from exploding capsules, using the pressure built up in its bottle-shaped sporophyte to literally shoot spores several inches into the air - making it one of nature's tiniest cannons!
confusionNotes: With only 3 recorded observations in all of New England, you're more likely to find almost any other small moss! However, the bottle-shaped sporophyte is so distinctive that once you see it, there's really nothing else it could be. Remember the rhyme: 'If it looks like a tiny bottle, you've found something quite a model!'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'dung moss,' this family actually plays an important ecological role in nutrient cycling and isn't as gross as it sounds. The extreme rarity in New England likely reflects both habitat loss (fewer small farms with grazing animals) and the specialized nature of its growing requirements.
compareHints: Southern Dung Moss (Splachnum pensylvanicum) is the only other Splachnum species potentially found in New England, but it's even rarer and has a more elongated capsule that's less distinctly bottle-shaped. The collar at the base of the capsule is less pronounced in Southern Dung Moss, and it tends to prefer slightly different substrate conditions, often favoring carnivore rather than herbivore dung.

relatedSpecies.distinction: **[UNCERTAIN CLAIM]** Southern Dung Moss differs from its relative Cruet Collar-moss primarily in the shape and color of its capsule caps - Southern Dung Moss has broader, more umbrella-like caps in warmer colors (orange, red, yellow), while Cruet Collar-moss typically has more collar-like structures.
